title: Ezekiel 46:1–15
context: The LORD continues his instructions for worship in the temple vision. The inner east gate is shut on working days and opened on Sabbaths and new moons; the prince worships at its threshold while the priests prepare his offerings, and the people worship at the gate’s entrance (46:1–3). The LORD sets the Sabbath, new moon, festival, freewill, and daily offerings (46:4–15), and orders how prince and people move through the courts at the feasts (46:8–10). Several amounts differ from Numbers 28, and they are noted without harmonizing. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. The question of sacrifices in this vision is treated at 40:38–49 and 44:15–31. The prince is often read against the Davidic hope of 2 Samuel 7 and Ezekiel 34:24 and 37:25, though he also offers a sin offering for himself (45:22), and his identity is held with care. An ephah is about 22 liters, and a hin about 6.5 liters.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “The gate of the inner court that looks toward the east shall be shut the six working days; but on the Sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the new moon it shall be opened.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD continues his instructions: the inner east gate “shall be shut the six working days” but opened on the Sabbath and new moon. Arminian readers see ordered worship that marks holy time and the LORD’s presence with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see worship arranged by God’s command, with the Sabbath and new moon set apart. Readers in this tradition note the link with the shut east gate of 44:1–3, through which the glory of the LORD entered (43:4).

verses.text: The prince shall enter by the way of the porch of the gate outside, and shall stand by the post of the gate; and the priests shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, and he shall worship at the threshold of the gate. Then he shall go out, but the gate shall not be shut until the evening.
verses.arminianNotes: “The prince shall enter by the way of the porch of the gate outside … and he shall worship at the threshold of the gate.” Arminian readers note that the prince worships but does not offer the sacrifices himself, for the priests prepare them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the prince has an honored place yet stands at the threshold while the priests serve. Readers in this tradition see a distinction between civil leadership and priestly ministry carefully kept.

verses.text: The people of the land shall worship at the door of that gate before the LORD on the Sabbaths and on the new moons.
verses.arminianNotes: “The people of the land shall worship at the door of that gate before the LORD on the Sabbaths and on the new moons.” Arminian readers see the whole community included in worship, not only its leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people gathered before the LORD at appointed times. Readers in this tradition note that prince and people worship together, each in an ordered place, which pictures a community united in worship.

verses.text: The burnt offering that the prince shall offer to the LORD shall be on the Sabbath day, six lambs without defect and a ram without defect;
verses.arminianNotes: “The burnt offering that the prince shall offer to the LORD shall be on the Sabbath day, six lambs without defect and a ram without defect.” Arminian readers see the prince providing the Sabbath offering for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prince’s role in supplying offerings (45:17). Numbers 28:9 prescribes two lambs for the Sabbath, and readers in this tradition note that Ezekiel’s amounts differ without forcing the two into agreement.

verses.text: and the meal offering shall be an ephah for the ram, and the meal offering for the lambs as he is able to give, and a hin of oil to an ephah.
verses.arminianNotes: “… the meal offering shall be an ephah for the ram, and the meal offering for the lambs as he is able to give.” Arminian readers see a set measure joined with freedom to give according to ability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see fixed portions combined with generosity “as he is able to give.” Readers in this tradition note the balance between ordered worship and willing offering, a pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture.

verses.text: On the day of the new moon it shall be a young bull without defect, six lambs, and a ram. They shall be without defect.
verses.arminianNotes: “On the day of the new moon it shall be a young bull without defect, six lambs, and a ram.” Arminian readers see the new moon marked by a larger offering, honoring the LORD at the start of each month.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the monthly rhythm of worship. Numbers 28:11 prescribes two bulls, a ram, and seven lambs, and readers in this tradition note the difference from Ezekiel’s list without harmonizing them.

verses.text: He shall prepare a meal offering: an ephah for the bull, and an ephah for the ram, and for the lambs according as he is able, and a hin of oil to an ephah.
verses.arminianNotes: “He shall prepare a meal offering: an ephah for the bull, and an ephah for the ram, and for the lambs according as he is able.” Arminian readers see grain offerings accompanying the animal sacrifices as part of complete worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the meal offerings completing the new moon worship. Readers in this tradition note the repeated phrase “as he is able,” which joins prescribed order with willing provision.

verses.text: When the prince enters, he shall go in by the way of the porch of the gate, and he shall go out by its way.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the prince enters, he shall go in by the way of the porch of the gate, and he shall go out by its way.” Arminian readers see the prince’s movements ordered, honoring the holiness of the gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see careful regulation of the prince’s access. Readers in this tradition note the parallel with 44:3, where the prince enters and leaves by the porch of the gate.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But when the people of the land come before the LORD in the appointed feasts, he who enters by the way of the north gate to worship shall go out by the way of the south gate; and he who enters by the way of the south gate shall go out by the way of the north gate. He shall not return by the way of the gate by which he came in, but shall go out straight before him.
verses.arminianNotes: “… he who enters by the way of the north gate to worship shall go out by the way of the south gate.” Arminian readers see orderly movement through the courts at the feasts, so that the crowds pass through without confusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a practical arrangement for large festival gatherings. Some readers also see a symbolic point in going “straight before him,” though readers in this tradition hold any symbolic meaning lightly.

verses.text: The prince shall go in with them when they go in. When they go out, he shall go out.
verses.arminianNotes: “The prince shall go in with them when they go in. When they go out, he shall go out.” Arminian readers see the prince worshiping among the people, sharing their movements rather than standing apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prince identified with the people in worship. Readers in this tradition note the humility of a ruler who enters and leaves with the congregation, under the same order of worship.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In the feasts and in the appointed holidays, the meal offering shall be an ephah for a bull, and an ephah for a ram, and for the lambs as he is able to give, and a hin of oil to an ephah.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the feasts and in the appointed holidays, the meal offering shall be an ephah for a bull, and an ephah for a ram, and for the lambs as he is able to give.” Arminian readers see consistent provisions for every feast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the same measures applied throughout the year. Readers in this tradition note that regular, ordered worship is a gift that shapes the community’s life before God.

verses.text: When the prince prepares a free will offering, a burnt offering or peace offerings as a free will offering to the LORD, one shall open for him the gate that looks toward the east; and he shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, as he does on the Sabbath day. Then he shall go out; and after his going out one shall shut the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: “When the prince prepares a free will offering … one shall open for him the gate that looks toward the east.” Arminian readers see room for voluntary devotion beyond the required offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the freewill offering honored. Readers in this tradition note that the east gate is opened for this offering and shut again afterward, keeping the gate’s special holiness.

verses.text: “ ‘ “You shall prepare a lamb a year old without defect for a burnt offering to the LORD daily. Morning by morning you shall prepare it.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall prepare a lamb a year old without defect for a burnt offering to the LORD daily. Morning by morning you shall prepare it.” Arminian readers see daily worship sustaining the community’s life before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a continual offering. Numbers 28:3–4 prescribes lambs both morning and evening, while Ezekiel mentions morning only, and readers in this tradition note that difference without harmonizing it.

verses.text: You shall prepare a meal offering with it morning by morning, the sixth part of an ephah, and the third part of a hin of oil to moisten the fine flour; a meal offering to the LORD continually by a perpetual ordinance.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall prepare a meal offering with it morning by morning … a meal offering to the LORD continually by a perpetual ordinance.” Arminian readers see daily devotion expressed in the grain offering that accompanies the lamb.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the perpetual ordinance of daily worship. Readers in this tradition take the vision as a literal future temple, a symbolic picture of God dwelling with his people, or a fulfillment in Christ and the church, without one reading settling the rest.

verses.text: Thus they shall prepare the lamb, the meal offering, and the oil, morning by morning, for a continual burnt offering.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Thus they shall prepare the lamb, the meal offering, and the oil, morning by morning, for a continual burnt offering.” Some Arminian readers who expect a literal future temple see memorial offerings here, while others read them as Ezekiel’s picture of restored worship fulfilled in Christ’s “one sacrifice for sins forever” (Hebrews 10:12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise divide. Some expect memorial or purifying offerings in a literal future temple, while many read the daily offering as restored worship in the terms of Ezekiel’s day, fulfilled in Christ’s single offering (Hebrews 10:1–14). Both views appear in each tradition.
